votes.why: the giant rock arches look like repeated variants of the same 3D asset.
procedural-looking fantasy landscape (repeated stone-arch textures, scattered pebble instancing, simple creature models) typical of a Vue/Terragen-style stock CG render rather than film-grade detail
the visibly faceted and stretched geometry of the giant curved rock arches despite detailed PBR foreground reflections
the giant stone arches repeat the same blocky surface pattern at visibly different scales.

The cinematic composition and atmosphere are strong, but the rock surfaces have stretched, repetitive procedural-looking texture and the creatures are simple, which reads as a high-end hobbyist or stock-style render (Terragen-like) rather than a film frame.
the foreground roots have a uniform rubbery sheen that makes the scene look rendered.

cinematic-quality fantasy environment (detailed desiccated creature carcass on root-covered cliff, atmospheric depth haze with giant arching rock formations) suggests a high-end film/cinematic, though it could be a polished standalone render.

the combination of a detailed sculpted alien carcass and atmospheric lighting with unpolished low-poly foreground rocks and smooth ribbon-like seaweed that fall short of top-budget film or AAA cinematic quality.
the foreground vines look like smooth, sharply folded plastic ribbons rather than organic growth.

the dense, detailed art direction (desiccated creature draped in roots, giant rock arches in atmospheric haze, wet-sand reflections) with filmic depth of field and lighting reads as a big-budget game cinematic or film frame, though some soft, repeated textures keep it from being certain.
the three creatures look like copies of the same 3D model posed at different distances.
polished but hobbyist-style creature render (Blender-like) with repeated duplicated creatures and somewhat generic rock/water materials rather than film-grade integration
the foreground creature's tendrils and legs pierce the shallow water with no ripples, meniscus, or wetness on the skin despite the otherwise polished lighting and sculpting.
the creatures’ legs meet the water without visibly disturbing it, as if the models were placed on a reflective surface.

the alien wading creatures have detailed skin, wing and feather textures, and the wet sand reflects the light with cinematic atmospheric depth, which looks like film-quality concept or cinematic work. The slightly soft reflections and some CG look keep me from being surer.
the visibly stretched textures along the foreground cliff ledges.
stretched procedural textures and smeared displacement artifacts on the cliffs and instanced creatures look like an ordinary hobbyist/stock 3D render, not film-grade or photographic.
the flat lighting and weak contact shadows where the repeated creature models meet the procedural rock ledges
the foreground ledges have visibly stretched textures that smear down their vertical faces.

the rock and ground textures are stretched and smeared like procedural or displacement artifacts, and the bird models are crude, which fits an ordinary or hobbyist 3D render rather than a film or photo. The soft sky and offline-render lighting keep it out of (d).
the foreground creatures look like duplicated models with the same pale, plasticky shading.
decent water simulation but the plain, flatly shaded creatures and repeated rock textures look like a hobbyist/stock 3D render rather than film-level integration.
the stiff plastic-looking winged creatures with thin stick-like legs and the abrupt seam where the crashing wave meets the flat reflective shore
the repeated winged creatures look like stiff models pasted in front of the surf.

The creatures are stiff, semi-transparent and pasted-looking, and the rocks are blurry and repetitive. The spray and cloud work is good, so it reads as a competent but unpolished CG render, not a top-budget production.
